pos: n. (proper name; a man of Aroer, in the roll of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew 'Aro'eri, the gentilic of Aroer. The place-name is connected with a word for a shrub of the desert, and three different Aroers are named in Scripture; which of them is meant here is not stated.
biblical_def: The Aroerite appears once, at the close of David's roll of mighty men: “Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jehiel the sons of Hothan the Aroerite” (1 Chronicles 11:44). Hothan is named only as a father, and his two sons only as his sons, and all three only by the town they came from. This is the ordinary way of that chapter. The thirty are listed again and again by their villages — the Tekoite, the Antothite, the Baharumite, the Shaalbonite — and the effect of reading the list straight through is of a muster roll read aloud. These were not a caste. They came from scattered towns on both sides of Jordan, some of them from places Israel barely held, and they came to Hebron with one purpose: “All these men of war, that could keep rank, came with a perfect heart to Hebron, to make David king over all Israel” (1 Chronicles 12:38). The Aroerite's sons are in the list because they came. Scripture keeps the names of men whose whole recorded act was to stand with the LORD's anointed when he had not yet been crowned, and that is honour enough to be written in a book that will outlast every throne.

corruption_summary: Lists of fighting men are read as royal propaganda; Chronicles presents them as men who came before there was a throne to profit by.
corruption_paragraphs: Rolls of a king's warriors are conventionally treated as court literature composed to flatter a dynasty. The detail of this list cuts against the reading. The men are identified by obscure villages, several of them outside Judah, many of them never mentioned again, and the chapter frames their coming as a strengthening of David in his kingdom before the kingdom was his in fact.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God records the service of the unknown. Hothan the Aroerite is a name, a town, and two sons. He is in Scripture because he stood where he ought to have stood. The Lord who promised that a cup of cold water would not lose its reward keeps books of exactly this kind.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Ashtaroth, in the roll of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ashterati, the gentilic of Ashtaroth, a city of Bashan east of Jordan. The town's name is the plural of Ashtoreth, the Canaanite goddess whose worship Israel was commanded to destroy.
biblical_def: The Ashterathite is named once: “Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jehiel the sons of Hothan the Aroerite” (1 Chronicles 11:44). The striking thing is the town. Ashtaroth was a city of Og king of Bashan, and it bore the name of Ashtoreth — the goddess for whose sake Solomon's heart was turned and whose groves Josiah tore down. Uzzia came out of a place named for an idol, and he stands in the roll of the men who made David king. Scripture lets the name stand without comment, and the restraint is instructive. It does not clean up his origin or give him a better address. A man is not disqualified by the town that bred him. Ashtaroth was given to the Levites out of Manasseh's portion, and the LORD who commanded Israel to break down the altars of that place also took a man out of it for the service of His anointed. “Such were some of you: but ye are washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11) is the New Testament form of the same mercy. The register of the mighty men contains a man whose home town was named after a demon, and it does not blush.

corruption_summary: A man's origin is treated as his identity; Scripture names the idolatrous town and seats the man among the faithful anyway.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern identity-talk makes a man's background the deepest truth about him, so that where he comes from settles what he is. The roll of David's mighty men contradicts it in a single line. Uzzia is the Ashterathite, out of a city named for Ashtoreth, and he is in the list of those who made David king. The text neither hides the origin nor treats it as decisive.

The principle to recover is that grace relocates a man without rewriting his history. Scripture is willing to call him by the idol-town because the town no longer rules him. “Such were some of you: but ye are washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11) says both halves: what he was is told plainly, and what he is now is owed to God and not to his birthplace.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Bahurim, in the roll of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Barchumi at 2 Samuel 23:31, generally understood as a transposed form of Bacharumi, the gentilic of Bahurim; 1 Chronicles 11:33 gives the regular form Baharumite.
biblical_def: The Barhumite is named once: “Abialbon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite” (2 Samuel 23:31). The Chronicler's parallel list spells the same man's town the regular way, “Azmaveth the Baharumite” (1 Chronicles 11:33), so the two forms stand for one gentilic with two Hebrew letters transposed. The dictionary records the variation without alarm; the Masoretic text preserves both spellings and nothing doctrinal hangs on either. Bahurim itself is a village on the road east out of Jerusalem, and Scripture remembers it for two bitter scenes: Shimei came out of Bahurim to curse David and cast stones at him as the king fled from Absalom, and the two messengers who carried Hushai's counsel hid in a well at Bahurim under a woman's spread covering. So Azmaveth's town is a place of both cursing and concealment, of a man who reviled the king and a household that saved his cause. One village furnished David both. That is how a place commonly stands in Scripture — not as a character but as ground where men of opposite hearts lived side by side.

corruption_summary: Variant spellings in parallel lists are urged as proof of textual corruption; they are ordinary orthographic variation that touches no doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: A name spelled Barhumite in Samuel and Baharumite in Chronicles is routinely offered as evidence that the text has decayed past trusting. The dictionary holds providential preservation through the Masoretic tradition and reads the pair as what it is: two letters transposed in a gentilic, with the same man, the same town and the same roll in both places. Nothing is in doubt but the order of two consonants.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is a right doctrine of preservation. The promise is that God's word shall not pass away, not that no scribe's hand ever slipped over a consonant. A reader who cannot hold both will either deny the obvious or distrust the Scripture; the confessional position denies neither.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Beth-arabah, in the roll of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew 'Arbati, the gentilic of Arabah or Beth-arabah, a place in the wilderness of Judah near the Jordan rift. The root 'arabah means a desert plain or waste.
biblical_def: The Arbathite appears twice, in the two parallel rolls of David's mighty men: “Abialbon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite” (2 Samuel 23:31), and “Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite” (1 Chronicles 11:32). The man's personal name differs between the lists — Abialbon in Samuel, Abiel in Chronicles — while his town holds steady. He came from the Arabah, the great desert trough running down to the Dead Sea, a country of salt and heat where Beth-arabah sat on the border of Judah and Benjamin. It is the bleakest address in the roll. The men David gathered in the cave and the wilderness were largely men with nothing: “every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented” (1 Samuel 22:2). Out of that company came the thirty. The Arbathite is one of them — a man of the waste ground who ended in the register of Israel's bravest. God's habit of recruiting from the wilderness is not incidental; it is how He staffed the kingdom of His anointed, and how He staffs it still.

corruption_summary: David's band is read as a bandit gang legitimised later; Scripture presents it as the LORD gathering a kingdom from the destitute.
corruption_paragraphs: David's wilderness following is often described as an outlaw troop whose later respectability was manufactured by royal scribes. 1 Samuel 22:2 is franker than any critic: the men were in distress, in debt, discontented. Scripture volunteers the unflattering fact, which is not the behaviour of a document covering its tracks, and then records what God made of them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God builds with what the world discards. “But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Corinthians 1:27). The thirty began as four hundred desperate men in a cave, and the Arbathite out of the salt waste is one of the names that came through.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Anathoth, in the rolls of David's men)
etymology: Hebrew 'Annetothi, the gentilic of Anathoth, a priestly city of Benjamin a few miles north of Jerusalem. Elsewhere the Authorized Version spells the same gentilic Anetothite and Anethothite.
biblical_def: The Antothite is named twice, of two different men: “Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Antothite” (1 Chronicles 11:28), and among the men who came to David at Ziklag, “and Berachah, and Jehu the Antothite” (1 Chronicles 12:3). Anathoth was one of the cities given to the priests out of Benjamin's portion (Joshua 21:18), and two men of it stood with David before he was king. Its great name, though, comes four centuries later. “The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah, of the priests that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin” (Jeremiah 1:1) — the weeping prophet was an Anathoth man, and his own townsmen were among those who sought his life. Solomon had sent Abiathar the priest home to Anathoth under sentence of deposition, and the town carried that history. So the gentilic gathers up a strange inheritance: a deposed priest, two of David's warriors, and the prophet of the exile. A single small town supplies Scripture with men who stood, a man who was put down, and a man who was hated at home for telling the truth.

corruption_paragraphs: There is a sentimental assumption that a true man of God will be recognised first by his own people. Anathoth gave Jeremiah the reverse: the men of his own town plotted against his life, and he was the loneliest man in the Old Testament. Christ made the pattern explicit at Nazareth: “No prophet is accepted in his own country” (Luke 4:24).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faithfulness is not measured by local reception. Two Antothites stood with David when standing with David was dangerous; a third Anathoth man preached forty years to a nation that would not hear and a town that wanted him dead. The register and the prophecy both come out of the same four-city Levitical grant.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Bahurim, in the roll of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Bacharumi, the regular gentilic of Bahurim. 2 Samuel 23:31 gives the same man's town in the transposed form Barhumite.
biblical_def: The Baharumite is named once: “Azmaveth the Baharumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite” (1 Chronicles 11:33). This is the regular spelling of the gentilic that 2 Samuel 23:31 gives as Barhumite, and the man is the same Azmaveth in both rolls. His village, Bahurim, lies on the ascent east of Jerusalem, and the reader of Samuel has already been there. It is where Shimei came out to curse the fleeing king, pelting him with stones and dust, and where David forbade Abishai to take the man's head: “let him alone, and let him curse; for the LORD hath bidden him” (2 Samuel 16:11). The town of one of David's own thirty is the town of David's loudest reviler. The king passed through it in the worst hour of his life and would not avenge himself there. That is the scene behind this quiet name in a list. A man of Bahurim stood among the mighty; another man of Bahurim cursed the anointed; and the LORD's anointed, going up the mount barefoot and weeping, left the judgment of both where it belonged.

corruption_summary: Patient endurance of reviling is read as weakness; David treats it as submission to the hand of God.
corruption_paragraphs: A king who lets a man curse him in the road is easily read as merely beaten, and David's restraint at Bahurim is sometimes reduced to political calculation. His own words give the reason, and it is theological: the LORD has bidden him, and it may be the LORD will requite good for the cursing. David received Shimei's stones as providence before he received them as insult.

The principle to recover is that providence governs even the mouth of an enemy. “Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again” (1 Peter 2:23) is said of Christ and is the standard for the Christian. The man of Bahurim who cursed and the man of Bahurim who fought for David both belonged to the same providence, and David left each where he belonged.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Bethel)
etymology: Hebrew Beth-ha'eli, the gentilic of Bethel, house of God — the town where Jacob saw the ladder and which Jeroboam afterward made a shrine for one of his golden calves.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, and it carries a curse: “In his days did Hiel the Bethelite build Jericho: he laid the foundation thereof in Abiram his firstborn, and set up the gates thereof in his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Joshua the son of Nun” (1 Kings 16:34). Five hundred years earlier Joshua had sworn an oath over the ruins: cursed be the man that buildeth this city Jericho; he shall lay the foundation in his firstborn and set up the gates in his youngest son (Joshua 6:26). Hiel built, and both sons died, and the historian records it as the fulfilling of a word spoken half a millennium before. The detail that he was a Bethelite sharpens it. Bethel means house of God, and by Hiel's day Bethel was Jeroboam's calf-shrine, the chief centre of the northern apostasy. A man of the house of God, out of the town that had turned God's house into an idol's, defied an ancient oath and paid for it with his children. “Be not deceived; God is not mocked” (Galatians 6:7). A curse does not expire because the generation that heard it has died.

corruption_summary: Ancient curses are read as superstition retrospectively fitted to events; Scripture presents the word spoken and the word performed.
corruption_paragraphs: The usual handling makes Joshua's oath a later insertion written backward from Hiel's misfortune, so that prophecy becomes editorial tidying. The dictionary holds the historicity of both texts and the reality of the word spoken. The narrator of Kings makes the claim explicitly — according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Joshua — and the claim is either true or the book is lying about its own subject.

The principle to recover is the durability of God's word across centuries. Five hundred years lay between the curse and its execution, and the delay altered nothing. “Hath he said, and shall he not do it?” (Numbers 23:19). Men presume on long silence as though it were acquittal; Hiel the Bethelite is Scripture's standing answer to that presumption.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Bethshemesh)
etymology: Hebrew Beth-shimshi, the gentilic of Bethshemesh, house of the sun — a Levitical city in the Judean lowland on the border toward Philistia.
biblical_def: The Bethshemite is named twice, both times of the same man and the same field: “And the cart came into the field of Joshua, a Bethshemite, and stood there, where there was a great stone” (1 Samuel 6:14), and again at verse 18, which notes that the stone remained to the writer's own day “in the field of Joshua, the Bethshemite.” The Philistines, plagued for seven months, had set the ark on a new cart behind two milch kine and let it go, and the kine took the straight road to Bethshemesh, lowing as they went. The harvesters looked up and saw the ark of the LORD coming home across their wheat. What follows is the sobering half. The men of Bethshemesh looked into the ark and God smote them, and the survivors asked, “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?” (1 Samuel 6:20). Joshua the Bethshemite is remembered for a field, a great stone, and a day when joy turned to terror because men handled holy things as though they were common. The ark came back of itself; it did not come back tame.

corruption_summary: Divine holiness is recast as a temperament God has outgrown; the ark at Bethshemesh is the text that forbids it.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern religious instinct treats God's holiness as a severity belonging to an earlier stage of revelation, since softened. Bethshemesh is where that instinct breaks. The same chapter that shows men rejoicing over the returning ark shows men struck down for looking into it, and the inspired comment is not that God overreacted but that He is holy.

The principle to recover is the fear of the LORD. “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?” is the right question, and the gospel answer is not that the holiness was exaggerated but that Christ has made a way into the holiest by His blood (Hebrews 10:19-20). Reverence is not abolished by grace; it is grounded in it.
roots_summary: Hebrew Beth-shimshi, the gentilic of Bethshemesh, house of the sun; Joshua the Bethshemite, in whose field the ark returned.
roots_lines: Hebrew Beth-shimshi, a gentilic formed from the place-name Bethshemesh.
Bethshemesh is beth (house) plus shemesh (sun): house of the sun.
It was a Levitical city in the lowland of Judah toward Philistia.
Joshua the Bethshemite owned the field where the ark's cart stopped.
The great stone of that field remained a landmark in the writer's day.
usage: the field of Joshua, a Bethshemite
they lifted up their eyes, and saw the ark, and rejoiced to see it
Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Elkosh, the designation of Nahum the prophet)
etymology: Hebrew 'Elqoshi, the gentilic of Elkosh, a place not otherwise named in Scripture and not now identifiable with certainty. Sites in Galilee, in Judah, and in Assyria have each been proposed.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, and it is the whole of what Scripture tells us about a prophet's origin: “The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite” (Nahum 1:1). No father is named, no king's reign is given to date him, no town is identifiable. Nahum is a voice and a gentilic. What he was given to say is the destruction of Nineveh, the capital of the empire that had carried Israel away, and he says it in three chapters of the most concentrated poetry in the prophets. But before the judgment he sets the ground of it: “The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked” (Nahum 1:3), and then, in the middle of the burden, the sweetest sentence in the book: “The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him” (Nahum 1:7). That is how a prophet of vengeance speaks, because the vengeance and the stronghold are the same attribute faced from two sides. Nineveh fell in 612 BC, as he said. The man himself remains the Elkoshite, and nothing more.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Elkoshite is a Hebrew gentilic and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.
webster_full: Elkoshite is a Hebrew proper name; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.
The name appears once, in Nahum 1:1.
It denotes a man of Elkosh, and designates Nahum the prophet.
Elkosh is named nowhere else in Scripture and is not securely identified.
It is the only biographical detail the book gives about its author.
scriptures: Nah 1:1
The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.
Nah 1:3
The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
Nah 1:7
The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.
Nah 3:7
And it shall come to pass, that all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say, Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee?
corruption_summary: Prophecies of judgment are read as nationalist resentment; Nahum grounds the burden in God's goodness to those who trust Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Oracles against foreign powers are commonly explained as the resentment of a small nation given religious dress, with Nahum treated as the most vindictive of the twelve. The book will not support it. The burden opens with the character of God — slow to anger, great in power — and reaches its centre not in a threat but in a refuge: the LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble.

The principle to recover is that judgment and mercy are one perfection. The God who will not at all acquit the wicked is the God who knoweth them that trust in Him, and Nahum sets the two sentences four verses apart deliberately. A reader who takes only the vengeance has read half the chapter; a reader who takes only the stronghold has read a different half and understood neither.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Elqoshi, the gentilic of Elkosh; the sole designation given of Nahum, prophet of Nineveh's fall.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Elqoshi, a gentilic formed from the place-name Elkosh.
Elkosh is named only here and cannot be securely located.
Sites in Galilee, Judah and Assyria have each been proposed.
The name is the only biographical detail the book of Nahum supplies.
Nahum's burden is the destruction of Nineveh, which fell in 612 BC.
usage: the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite
the LORD is slow to anger, and great in power
a strong hold in the day of trouble

pos: n. (proper name; the people of Ashdod, one of the five Philistine cities)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ashdodim, the gentilic plural of Ashdod. The Authorized Version also renders the people Ashdothites at Joshua 13:3, and the speech of the city Ashdod at Nehemiah 13:24.
biblical_def: The Ashdodites appear once by that name, in the muster of Jerusalem's enemies: “But it came to pass, that when Sanballat, and Tobiah, and the Arabians, and the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites, heard that the walls of Jerusalem were made up, and that the breaches began to be stopped, then they were very wroth” (Nehemiah 4:7). Ashdod was one of the five Philistine cities — the one whose temple of Dagon the ark had emptied, where the idol fell on his face before it and was found broken on the threshold. Centuries later its people are still ranged against the work of God, now in a coalition of four peoples with no common cause but the walls going up. Nehemiah's answer is the pattern for every such hour: “Nevertheless we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night” (Nehemiah 4:9). Prayer and a watch; neither without the other. And the deeper menace from Ashdod was not the sword but the marriage-bed — Nehemiah found Jewish children speaking Ashdod's language because their fathers had married Ashdod's daughters (Nehemiah 13:23-24). The wall held. The households did not, and that is the harder war.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Ashdodites is a Hebrew gentilic and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.
webster_full: Ashdodites is a Hebrew proper name; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.
The name appears once, in Nehemiah 4:7.
It denotes the people of Ashdod, one of the five Philistine cities.
Joshua 13:3 renders the same people Ashdothites.
Nehemiah 13:24 speaks of children who spake the speech of Ashdod.
scriptures: Neh 4:7

But it came to pass, that when Sanballat, and Tobiah, and the Arabians, and the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites, heard that the walls of Jerusalem were made up, and that the breaches began to be stopped, then they were very wroth,
Neh 4:9
Nevertheless we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night, because of them.
And their children spake half in the speech of Ashdod, and could not speak in the Jews' language, but according to the language of each people.
And when they of Ashdod arose early on the morrow, behold, Dagon was fallen upon his face to the earth before the ark of the LORD. And they took Dagon, and set him in his place again.
corruption_summary: Intermarriage with the surrounding nations is treated as harmless openness; Nehemiah names it as the loss of a generation's tongue.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah's action against the foreign marriages is among the most disliked passages in the book, read as xenophobia. The text gives his reason, and it is not blood but covenant: the children could no longer speak the language in which the law was read to them. A household that cannot understand Scripture has been conquered without a siege, and Nehemiah saw the walls he had built made pointless by the marriages inside them.

The principle to recover is that the household is the front line. Ashdod's army failed at the wall and Ashdod's daughters succeeded in the home. “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14) is the New Testament form of the same guard, and it is a mercy to children before it is a restriction on parents.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Ashdodim, the gentilic plural of Ashdod, a Philistine city; named among Jerusalem's enemies in Nehemiah 4.

Ashdod was one of the five cities of the Philistine lords.
Joshua 13:3 renders the people Ashdothites.
Dagon's temple at Ashdod is where the idol fell before the ark, 1 Samuel 5.
Nehemiah 13:24 records children speaking half in the speech of Ashdod.
